title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can serve as a useful source of feedback for complex writing tasks and how its feedback compares with peer-generated feedback. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves essay writing directly, but whether the feedback it produces differs in quality and characteristics from student peer feedback, and whether essay quality is associated with feedback quality from either source.

The study used ChatGPT as a feedback provider in an online argumentative essay-writing module. Students wrote essays first, then provided peer feedback and also received ChatGPT-generated feedback using essentially the same prompt. The feedback was coded with established schemes covering affective, cognitive, and constructive dimensions, while essays were coded for argumentative quality. The sample included 74 graduate students in food sciences at a Dutch university, and the work was conducted over two weeks in an online Brightspace module with the FeedbackFruits peer-feedback tool.

Results showed that peer feedback was overall higher quality than ChatGPT feedback, mainly because peers were better at identifying problems in the essays, while ChatGPT produced more descriptive summaries. There was no overall significant relationship between essay quality and feedback quality for either peers or ChatGPT, although some small correlations appeared for affective feedback features. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may complement peer feedback rather than replace it, especially for large writing-intensive courses, but they also note that prompt wording, model behavior, and validation of AI-generated feedback require further study.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's generative AI chatbot based on GPT-family large language models, capable of producing natural-language responses and feedback from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as a feedback source on students' argumentative essays. The paper provided ChatGPT the same feedback prompt given to peers (with minor wording changes) and compared the quality of ChatGPT-generated feedback with peer feedback.

findings.finding_summary: In a sample of 74 graduate students, ChatGPT-generated feedback differed significantly from peer feedback. ChatGPT scored higher on description (M=2.00, SD=0.00) but lower on identification of problems (M=1.29, SD=0.70) than peer feedback (description M=1.91, SD=0.29; identification M=1.52, SD=0.49), while affective, justification, and constructive components did not differ significantly.
findings.measure: Feedback quality coding scheme: affective, description, identification, justification, constructive components
findings.effect_size: eta2=0.03 for description; eta2=0.02 for identification

findings.finding_summary: There was no significant overall relationship between essay quality and ChatGPT-generated feedback quality. A positive correlation appeared between essay quality and the affective feature of ChatGPT feedback for some essay elements, while a negative relationship appeared for justification on one essay element; the overall correlation was not significant.
findings.measure: Spearman correlations between essay quality and ChatGPT feedback quality/features

quality_tier_rationale: This is a single-institution exploratory study with correlational and group-comparison analyses, not a randomized trial. The methodology is clear and coder reliability is reported, but the evidence is limited by the small sample and one-course context.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports statistically significant differences, but the effects are small (eta2=.02-.03) and the practical impact is mixed. Overall influence on feedback quality is suggestive rather than strong.
